events.title: Valentinian I and Valens become emperors
events.summary: The army at Nicaea chose Valentinian, a Pannonian guards officer, as emperor on 26 February 364; on 28 March at the Hebdomon outside Constantinople he made his younger brother Valens co-Augustus, and at Mediana near Naissus they divided the court, army and empire, Valentinian taking the West and Valens the East.
events.detail: The division of army units and officials between the brothers, recorded by Ammianus, anticipated the permanent split of 395 and gave many units paired seniores and iuniores names in the Notitia Dignitatum. Valentinian's court was based mainly at Trier and Milan, Valens' at Constantinople, Antioch and Marcianople.
scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire: Valens and the Roman State in the Fourth Century AD (2002)

events.title: Revolt of Procopius
events.summary: Procopius, a maternal relative of Julian rumoured to have been designated his successor, emerged from hiding and was proclaimed emperor in Constantinople while Valens was away; he won over units passing through Thrace by displaying Constantius II's widow Faustina and her infant daughter, last of the Constantinian line.
events.detail: He gained Thrace, Bithynia and support from the Gothic Tervingi, who sent 3,000 men; this later gave Valens his pretext for the Gothic war of 367.

events.title: The Cretan earthquake and tsunami
events.summary: A massive earthquake off western Crete, estimated at magnitude 8 or more, uplifted the western end of the island by up to 9 m and sent a tsunami across the eastern Mediterranean; Ammianus describes the sea withdrawing at Alexandria and ships being hurled onto rooftops.
events.detail: The anniversary was commemorated at Alexandria as a 'day of horror' into the sixth century. Geological evidence of the uplift is visible on the Cretan coast; destruction across Crete, Cyprus, Sicily and Libya was later conflated in literary sources.
events.locName: Off western Crete; tsunami at Alexandria and across the eastern Mediterranean
scholarship: Kelly, 'Ammianus and the great tsunami', JRS 94 (2004)
Shaw et al., 'Eastern Mediterranean tectonics and tsunami hazard inferred from the AD 365 earthquake', Nature Geoscience 1 (2008)

events.title: Battles of Thyatira and Nacolia
events.summary: Valens defeated Procopius' general Gomoarius at Thyatira in Lydia, and in May 366 at Nacolia in Phrygia Procopius' remaining troops deserted after his commander Agilo defected; Procopius was betrayed and beheaded on 27 May 366.

sides.strength: Thracian and palatine units, Gothic auxiliaries

battle.significance: Ended the last Constantinian bid for power.

events.title: Damasus and Ursinus: the papal election riots
events.summary: After the death of Pope Liberius, rival factions elected Ursinus and Damasus as bishop of Rome; in the fighting, Damasus' supporters stormed the basilica of Sicininus and, Ammianus reports, 137 corpses were found there in a single day.
events.detail: Ammianus observes drily that the wealth of the Roman see, its gifts from matrons and its bishops riding in carriages and dining better than kings made the office worth killing for. Damasus prevailed with the support of the urban prefect, and went on to promote the cult of martyrs with verse inscriptions carved by Filocalus.

events.title: The 'Barbarian Conspiracy' in Britain
events.summary: In 367 Picts, Attacotti and Scotti attacked Britain while Franks and Saxons raided Gaul; the count of the Saxon Shore Nectaridus was killed and the dux Fullofaudes ambushed. Valentinian sent Count Theodosius (the Elder), who recovered London and restored order in 368-369.
events.detail: Ammianus calls it a 'barbarica conspiratio'; the frontier scouts (areani) were accused of collusion and disbanded. A province, Valentia, was created or renamed. The scale of the crisis is debated: some archaeologists see little destruction, but signal stations on the Yorkshire coast may date from the restoration.
scholarship: Esmonde Cleary, The Ending of Roman Britain (1989)
events.debate: Whether it was a coordinated 'conspiracy' and how much damage it caused.

events.title: Gratian proclaimed Augustus at Ambiani
events.summary: After a serious illness, Valentinian raised his eight-year-old son Gratian directly to Augustus (not Caesar) before the army at Ambiani (Amiens), securing the dynasty; the poet Ausonius became his tutor.

events.title: Battle of Solicinium
events.summary: Valentinian and Gratian led a punitive expedition across the Rhine after the Alamanni sacked Mogontiacum during a Christian festival; the Alamanni held a steep hill at Solicinium but were driven off with heavy losses after Valentinian nearly fell in an ambush.
events.detail: Valentinian then built an intensive system of forts, burgi and river crossings along the Rhine and Danube (369-374), the last great Roman frontier programme in the West.
events.locName: Solicinium (unidentified; perhaps near Rottenburg am Neckar or Heidelberg)

battle.significance: Punitive victory followed by major fortification programme.

events.title: Valens' Gothic war and the treaty on the Danube
events.summary: After three years of campaigns north of the Danube (367-369) against the Tervingi, hampered by floods in 368, Valens met the Tervingian 'judge' Athanaric on a boat in midstream, since Athanaric had sworn never to set foot on Roman soil; trade was restricted to two Danube towns and subsidies ended.
events.detail: Themistius' Oration 10 celebrates the peace as philanthropy. The treaty treated the Goths as an independent people. Athanaric followed it with a persecution of Gothic Christians (369-372), whose martyrs include Saba the Goth.
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)

events.title: Treason and magic trials at Rome and Antioch
events.summary: At Rome the prefect of the annona Maximinus (later praetorian prefect) prosecuted senators and their wives for adultery and magic with torture; at Antioch in 371-372 a séance using a magic tripod that spelled out THEOD as the next emperor's name led to the execution of the notary Theodorus and many others, and burnings of books.
events.detail: Ammianus, who was in Antioch and burned some of his own papers, gives a horrified account. The trials show the reach of imperial fear of divination in a precarious dynasty.
scholarship: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

events.title: Revolt of Firmus in Mauretania
events.summary: Firmus, son of the Moorish prince Nubel, rebelled after a dispute with the rapacious comes Africae Romanus; Count Theodosius waged a hard campaign through Mauretania until Firmus hanged himself to avoid capture.
events.detail: Firmus had Donatist support, and his brother Gildo, who fought for Rome, later held Africa (386-398). The campaign typifies the late Roman reliance on Moorish princes as both allies and rebels.

events.title: Ambrose elected bishop of Milan
events.summary: Ambrose, governor of Aemilia-Liguria, intervened to calm the crowds at the disputed election to succeed the Homoian bishop Auxentius, and was himself acclaimed bishop by the people, according to legend after a child cried 'Ambrose bishop'; he was baptised and consecrated within a week.
scholarship: McLynn, Ambrose of Milan: Church and Court in a Christian Capital (1994)

events.title: Death of Valentinian I at Brigetio
events.summary: After campaigning against the Quadi, who had invaded Pannonia in 374 after the murder of their king Gabinius by a Roman officer, Valentinian received a Quadic embassy at Brigetio, flew into a rage at their insolence and died of a stroke.
events.detail: Five days later the officers proclaimed his four-year-old son Valentinian II Augustus at Aquincum without consulting Gratian, who accepted the fait accompli. Count Theodosius was executed at Carthage early in 376 in murky circumstances; his son, the future Theodosius I, retired to Spain.

events.title: The Goths cross the Danube
events.summary: Driven by the Huns, who had destroyed the Greuthungian kingdom of Ermanaric and defeated Athanaric's Tervingi on the Dniester, a large body of Tervingi under Alavivus and Fritigern petitioned Valens for land and were admitted across the Danube, probably near Durostorum, in exchange for military service; the Greuthungi under Alatheus and Saphrax crossed without permission.
events.detail: Ammianus describes the crossing in boats, rafts and hollowed tree trunks, and the corrupt Roman officers Lupicinus and Maximus extorting the starving Goths, selling them dog meat in exchange for their children as slaves. Numbers are unknown: Eunapius' 200,000 is a guess; modern estimates for the Tervingi range from 15,000 to 20,000 warriors with families. Valens welcomed the prospect of recruits, which Ammianus regards as fatal optimism.
scholarship: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)
events.debate: Numbers of Goths and the role of the Huns (Heather) versus Roman policy and the internal politics of the Goths (Kulikowski, Halsall).

events.title: Lupicinus' banquet and the battle of Marcianople
events.summary: At a banquet at Marcianople the comes Lupicinus tried to seize or murder Fritigern and Alavivus; Fritigern escaped, rallied the Goths and destroyed Lupicinus' army nine miles from the city, beginning the Gothic war.

battle.significance: Turned the Gothic settlement into open war.

events.title: Battle of Ad Salices
events.summary: Roman forces under Richomeres, Profuturus and Trajanus fought the Goths behind their wagon-laager at Ad Salices ('By the Willows') in the Dobruja; the battle was bloody and indecisive, and Ammianus says the bones of the dead still whitened the field years later.

sides.strength: Gothic warriors behind the wagon circle

battle.significance: Showed the Goths could not be easily contained.

events.title: Battle of Argentaria
events.summary: Gratian's generals Nannienus and Mallobaudes, king of the Franks and comes domesticorum, destroyed the Lentienses, an Alamannic people who had crossed the frozen Rhine, near Argentaria (Horbourg near Colmar); Ammianus says only 5,000 of 40,000 escaped.
events.detail: The campaign delayed Gratian's march east to help Valens, a factor in Valens' decision to fight at Adrianople without waiting.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.summary: Valens, refusing to wait for Gratian, marched out from Adrianople in the August heat and attacked Fritigern's wagon camp; while negotiations dragged on, Roman units engaged prematurely, the returning Greuthungian cavalry of Alatheus and Saphrax struck the Roman left, and the infantry, crushed together so they could not draw swords, were annihilated. Valens died and two-thirds of the army perished.
events.detail: Ammianus counts the dead as including the generals Trajanus and Sebastianus, 35 tribunes and the former magister Equitius' relatives; he compares it to Cannae. Valens' body was never found; one story has him burned alive in a farmhouse. Modern estimates put the Roman army at 15,000-30,000 and losses at 10,000-20,000. The Goths failed to take Adrianople and Constantinople, where an Arab contingent of Queen Mavia's Saracens horrified them by drinking the blood of a slain Goth. Magister Julius ordered the massacre of Gothic recruits in the eastern provinces. Older views of Adrianople as a victory of cavalry over infantry, ushering in medieval warfare (Oman), are now rejected. Its consequences were political: Goths settled as an autonomous force within the empire.
events.locName: About 13 km north of Hadrianopolis (Edirne), Thrace

sides.losses: two-thirds of the army (Ammianus); emperor killed

sides.strength: Tervingi, Greuthungi and Alans; perhaps 15,000-20,000 warriors

battle.significance: Death of an emperor and destruction of the eastern field army; led to the settlement of Goths inside the empire.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Burns, 'The battle of Adrianople: a reconsideration', Historia 22 (1973)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
events.debate: Army sizes, battlefield location and the long-term military significance are disputed. Christian sources (Orosius) saw the 'Arian' emperor's death as divine punishment.

events.title: Theodosius made Augustus at Sirmium
events.summary: Gratian recalled Theodosius, son of the executed Count Theodosius, from his Spanish estates, gave him a command against the Goths and Sarmatians and proclaimed him Augustus of the East at Sirmium, together with the dioceses of Dacia and Macedonia.
events.detail: Theodosius rebuilt the eastern army by mass recruitment including barbarians, based himself at Thessalonica, and after a serious illness was baptised there in 380 by the Nicene bishop Acholius.

events.title: Edict of Thessalonica (Cunctos populos)
events.summary: Theodosius, Gratian and Valentinian II decreed that all peoples should follow the faith 'which the divine apostle Peter delivered to the Romans' as taught by Damasus of Rome and Peter of Alexandria, belief in the one deity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit; others were 'demented and insane' heretics.
events.detail: The edict, addressed to the people of Constantinople, defined orthodoxy by communion with named bishops and laid the legal foundation for Nicene Christianity as the state religion. On entering Constantinople in November 380 Theodosius expelled the Homoian bishop Demophilus and installed Gregory of Nazianzus.
scholarship: Errington, Roman Imperial Policy from Julian to Theodosius (2006)
events.debate: Whether the edict was an empire-wide religious law or a specific measure for Constantinople is debated (Errington).

events.title: First Council of Constantinople
events.summary: About 150 eastern bishops, summoned by Theodosius, reaffirmed the Nicene faith, condemned Macedonians (who denied the divinity of the Spirit) and others, and in canon 3 gave the bishop of Constantinople 'precedence of honour after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome'.
events.detail: Gregory of Nazianzus presided briefly after Meletius' death and then resigned amid quarrels; Nectarius, an unbaptised senator, succeeded him. The expanded creed attributed to this council (the 'Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed', the Nicene Creed of modern liturgies) is first attested at Chalcedon in 451. Canon 3 began the long rivalry of Constantinople with Alexandria and Rome.

sources.w: Canons of the Council of Constantinople (381)

events.title: Theodosius' treaty with the Goths
events.summary: On 3 October 382, after Theodosius' generals had contained but not defeated the Goths, the magister Saturninus made peace: the Goths were settled in northern Thrace and along the Danube as a people under their own leaders, providing troops under their own commanders while remaining legally autonomous.
events.detail: Themistius' Oration 16 justifies the peace as turning enemies into farmers and allies. The arrangement, whose exact terms are unrecorded, is often seen as the first settlement of an intact barbarian people on Roman soil, a precedent for the federate kingdoms of the fifth century. Heather and Kulikowski stress how much it was a compromise forced by Roman weakness. Athanaric had already come to Constantinople in January 381 and died there, receiving a state funeral.
events.locName: Constantinople; settlement in Thrace and Moesia
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)
Errington, 'Theodosius and the Goths', Chiron 26 (1996)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
events.debate: Terms of the foedus (autonomy, land vs tax shares) are unknown and debated.

events.title: Usurpation of Magnus Maximus and death of Gratian
events.summary: Magnus Maximus, a Spanish officer serving in Britain and a relative of Theodosius, was proclaimed emperor by the British army and crossed to Gaul; Gratian's troops deserted near Paris, and Gratian was caught and killed at Lugdunum on 25 August 383.
events.detail: Gratian had alienated the army by favouring his Alan bodyguard. Maximus ruled Gaul, Britain and Spain from Trier and was recognised by Theodosius in 384. Welsh legend (Macsen Wledig, 'The Dream of Macsen') made him an ancestor of Welsh dynasties; Gildas blamed him for stripping Britain of troops.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

events.title: The Altar of Victory controversy
events.summary: In 382 Gratian removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house and cut state funding of the pagan cults and the Vestals; in 384 the urban prefect Symmachus petitioned Valentinian II for its restoration in his Third Relatio, and Ambrose answered with two letters ensuring the request failed.
events.detail: Symmachus' plea, 'one cannot reach so great a mystery by one road alone', is a classic statement of religious pluralism. Gratian had also refused the title pontifex maximus (the exact date is debated, possibly 383 or later per Cameron).
scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)

events.title: Execution of Priscillian at Trier
events.summary: Priscillian, an ascetic bishop of Avila accused by Spanish bishops of Manichaeism and sorcery, was tried before Magnus Maximus at Trier and beheaded with several followers, including the noblewoman Euchrotia, the first Christians executed by Christian authorities for heresy.
events.detail: Martin of Tours and Ambrose protested; Martin refused communion with the accusing bishops Ithacius and Hydatius. Priscillianism survived in Galicia into the sixth century.
scholarship: Chadwick, Priscillian of Avila (1976)
Burrus, The Making of a Heretic (1995)

events.title: Ambrose and the Milan basilica conflict
events.summary: The empress mother Justina and the court of Valentinian II demanded a basilica in Milan for Homoian worship; Ambrose and his congregation occupied the church through Holy Week of 386, singing antiphonal hymns, while troops surrounded it, and the court backed down. Weeks later Ambrose discovered the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and installed them under the altar of his new basilica.
events.detail: Augustine, then teacher of rhetoric at Milan, witnessed the events (Confessions 9.7) and was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. Ambrose's hymns introduced congregational singing to the West.
scholarship: McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (1994)

events.title: Partition of Armenia between Rome and Persia
events.summary: Theodosius and Shapur III agreed to divide Armenia: the Persian zone (Persarmenia), about four-fifths of the kingdom, under Khosrov IV, and a smaller Roman zone in the west under Arsaces III, ending decades of struggle since Shapur II had captured King Arsaces II and Rome's protégé Pap had been murdered by a Roman officer (374/375).
events.detail: The partition brought nearly a century and a half of relative peace between the two empires. The Roman Arsacid kingdom was absorbed after Arsaces III's death around 390.
scholarship: Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II (2002)
Blockley, East Roman Foreign Policy (1992)

events.title: The Riot of the Statues at Antioch
events.summary: A new tax levy, perhaps for Theodosius' decennalia, provoked Antioch's crowd to smash the statues and portraits of the emperor and his family; facing imperial vengeance, the city was saved by the embassy of Bishop Flavian and the intercession of monks, while the young priest John Chrysostom preached his 21 Homilies on the Statues.
events.detail: Libanius' orations on the riot provide a pagan view. The episode illustrates the crime of lèse-majesté against images and the rising intercessory power of bishops and holy men in cities.
scholarship: Browning, 'The riot of AD 387 in Antioch', JRS 42 (1952)

events.title: Battle of Siscia
events.summary: After Magnus Maximus invaded Italy in 387, driving Valentinian II and Justina to Thessalonica, Theodosius marched west; at Siscia on the Save his Hunnic, Alan and Gothic horse archers swam the river and routed Maximus' army.
events.detail: Theodosius had married Valentinian's sister Galla, sealing the alliance. His army included large barbarian contingents, some of whom Maximus had tried to suborn.

sides.strength: eastern army with Gothic, Hunnic and Alan auxiliaries

events.title: Battle of Poetovio and death of Magnus Maximus
events.summary: Theodosius defeated Maximus' brother Marcellinus at Poetovio; Maximus was surrounded at Aquileia, handed over by his own troops, and executed on 28 August 388. His son Victor was killed in Gaul by the Frankish general Arbogast.
events.detail: Theodosius restored Valentinian II in the West under the supervision of Arbogast and stayed in Italy until 391, the period of his clashes with Ambrose.

battle.significance: Ended Maximus' regime; Theodosius effectively ruled the whole empire.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

events.title: The Callinicum synagogue affair
events.summary: Christians at Callinicum on the Euphrates, incited by their bishop, burned a synagogue and a Valentinian gnostic chapel; Theodosius ordered the bishop to rebuild the synagogue, but Ambrose refused to celebrate the Eucharist in the emperor's presence until he withdrew the order.

events.title: Massacre of Thessalonica and Theodosius' penance
events.summary: After the people of Thessalonica lynched the Gothic magister militum Butheric, who had jailed a popular charioteer for homosexual assault, troops were turned on the crowd in the hippodrome and some 7,000 were killed (Theodoret); Ambrose, in a private letter, required Theodosius to do public penance before readmitting him to communion.
events.detail: Later church historians dramatised the scene into Ambrose barring Theodosius at the cathedral door, an archetype for medieval church-state relations. Modern scholars (McLynn) see a carefully staged reconciliation that benefited both men. The casualty figure and the emperor's personal responsibility are uncertain.
scholarship: McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (1994)

events.title: Obelisk of Theodosius raised in the Hippodrome
events.summary: The prefect Proclus re-erected an obelisk of Thutmose III, brought from Karnak, on the spina of the Hippodrome of Constantinople in 32 days, as its Latin and Greek inscriptions boast; the marble base shows Theodosius and his family in the kathisma receiving tribute.

sources.w: Base of the Obelisk of Theodosius

events.title: Ammianus Marcellinus completes his Res Gestae
events.summary: Ammianus Marcellinus, a Greek-speaking former protector from Antioch living in Rome, completed his Latin history in 31 books from Nerva to the death of Valens (378); books 14-31, covering 353-378, survive and are the finest narrative history of late antiquity.
events.detail: Ammianus served on the staff of Ursicinus, escaped from Amida in 359 and marched with Julian into Persia; his work combines eyewitness reports, digressions (on Persia, the Huns, Roman society) and moral judgement. He admires Julian while criticising his superstition and school law, and is restrained about Christianity. Historians consider him the most reliable narrator of the fourth century, though Barnes (1998) and Kelly have stressed his literary artifice and selective silences.
scholarship: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)
Barnes, Ammianus Marcellinus and the Representation of Historical Reality (1998)
Kelly, Ammianus Marcellinus: The Allusive Historian (2008)
events.debate: Date of completion (c. 390-391); identification of Libanius' correspondent.

events.title: Destruction of the Serapeum and the Theodosian decrees
events.summary: Theodosius' laws of 24 February and 16 June 391 banned sacrifice and visits to temples; in Alexandria, rioting between pagans and Christians led by Bishop Theophilus ended with the destruction of the great Serapeum and its cult statue by Bryaxis, with imperial permission. A law of 8 November 392 banned all forms of pagan cult, even private household worship.
events.detail: Rufinus describes a soldier striking the statue's jaw with an axe while the crowd waited for the sky to fall. The Serapeum's 'daughter library' may already have been dispersed. The laws were not uniformly enforced, and pagan cult persisted in many places into the sixth century, but the decrees mark the legal end of public paganism.
scholarship: Hahn, Emmel and Gotter (eds.), From Temple to Church (2008)
Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
events.debate: Date of the Serapeum's destruction (391 or 392).

events.title: Death of Valentinian II; Eugenius proclaimed
events.summary: Valentinian II, aged 21 and humiliated by his magister militum Arbogast, who had torn up his letter of dismissal, was found hanged at Vienne; on 22 August Arbogast, unable as a Frank to take the throne himself, proclaimed the rhetor and court official Eugenius emperor.
events.detail: Whether Valentinian was murdered or took his own life was disputed even at the time; Ambrose's funeral oration hedges. Eugenius, a nominal Christian, restored funding to pagan cults at the request of the senatorial aristocracy led by Virius Nicomachus Flavianus, though Alan Cameron argues that the 'pagan revival' of 393-394 has been exaggerated.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)

events.title: End of the ancient Olympic Games (traditional)
events.summary: The ancient Olympic Games are traditionally said to have ended after the 293rd Olympiad in 393, under Theodosius' anti-pagan legislation, though no law specifically abolishing them is known.
events.detail: The Byzantine historian Cedrenus dates the end to Theodosius I, while a scholion to Lucian attributes the burning of the temple of Zeus to Theodosius II. Archaeological finds at Olympia (including a bronze victor list running to 385) and later evidence suggest that some form of the games continued into the fifth century.
scholarship: Remijsen, The End of Greek Athletics in Late Antiquity (2015)
events.debate: The date 393 is a modern convention; games probably continued until c. 420-430.

events.title: Battle of the Frigidus
events.summary: Theodosius forced the Julian Alps and attacked Eugenius and Arbogast on the river Frigidus (Vipava) on 5-6 September 394; on the first day his 20,000 Gothic federates under Gainas and Alaric were thrown back with heavy losses, but on the second a violent bora wind blew dust into the western army's faces and turned its missiles back, and part of Arbogast's force defected. Eugenius was captured and beheaded; Arbogast killed himself two days later.
events.detail: Christian writers (Rufinus, Ambrose, Orosius, Augustine) and the pagan poet Claudian alike celebrated the miraculous wind, Claudian's lines ('O nimium dilecte deo') later quoted by Augustine. Eugenius' army reportedly marched under statues of Jupiter and banners of Hercules; Flavianus committed suicide. The battle was framed as the last stand of paganism, a construction Cameron and others contest. The heavy Gothic losses (10,000 according to Orosius, who welcomed them) embittered Alaric. Theodosius died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the empire to his sons Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West under Stilicho's guardianship, a division that proved permanent.

sides.strength: eastern army with c. 20,000 Gothic federates
western army with Frankish and Alamannic contingents

battle.significance: Last time the whole empire was united under one emperor; traditionally the victory of Christianity over paganism.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans
Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius

scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
Kulikowski, The Tragedy of Empire: From Constantine to the Destruction of Roman Italy (2019)
events.debate: The religious framing of the battle; the wind as a natural bora vs miracle; numbers.

events.title: Composition of the Historia Augusta
events.summary: The Historia Augusta, a collection of imperial biographies from Hadrian to Carinus (117-284) purporting to be by six authors writing under Diocletian and Constantine, was in fact written by a single author around the 390s, as Hermann Dessau showed in 1889.
events.detail: The lives of the major emperors to Caracalla draw on a good source (probably Marius Maximus and an 'Ignotus'), but the later lives and those of usurpers and minor figures are increasingly fictional, with invented documents, letters, speeches and bogus authorities (Syme counted dozens of fake historians). For the third century, where other narratives are thin, it is both indispensable and treacherous: historians use it only where corroborated by coins, inscriptions or other texts. A gap covering 244-260 is either a lacuna or a deliberate fiction. Syme saw a 'rogue grammarian' amusing himself; Cameron and others place it in the context of pagan senatorial culture c. 395-400.
scholarship: Dessau, 'Über Zeit und Persönlichkeit der Scriptores Historiae Augustae', Hermes 24 (1889)
Syme, Ammianus and the Historia Augusta (1968)
Syme, Emperors and Biography (1971)
Rohrbacher, The Play of Allusion in the Historia Augusta (2016)
Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
events.debate: Date (from c. 360 to c. 410; most now c. 395-400), purpose (hoax, satire, pagan propaganda) and the value of the early lives.
